claims.text: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the relative kinetics of precursor decomposition, nucleation, and atomic diffusion.
Sufficiently rapid precursor decomposition creates instantaneous supersaturation of metal atoms.
Instantaneous supersaturation causes rapid, nearly simultaneous nucleation of the constituent metals.
Rapid nucleation suppresses, or leaves insufficient time for, elemental diffusion.
Suppressing elemental diffusion during particle formation prevents phase segregation and yields a homogeneous alloy.
Pronounced atomic diffusion can drive progressive phase separation in noble metal-containing high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
When nucleation is slow relative to diffusion, elemental segregation and phase separation occur.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneous mixture of noble metal salts or complexes on a support.
Changing the heating ramp while holding composition and atmosphere constant provides a controlled comparison of rapid and gradual precursor decomposition.
Rapid heating will produce a uniform, homogeneous alloy phase.
Rapid heating will produce nanoparticles with high surface-atom exposure.
High surface-atom exposure makes the resulting nanoparticles suitable for catalytic applications.
Slower processing will be more likely to produce phase separation and elemental segregation.
Slower processing will be more likely to produce uncontrolled particle morphology.
The kinetic-control hypothesis primarily applies to noble metal-based multimetal systems processed rapidly under non-equilibrium conditions.
Equilibrium thermodynamic effects can instead govern phase decomposition in some high-entropy alloy systems.
The kinetic threshold for homogeneous alloy formation may vary with particle size, composition, and processing details.
A slow-heating condition producing homogeneous particles with surface exposure comparable to or greater than the rapid-heating condition would falsify the claimed necessity of rapid processing.

contradictions.description: The prediction is probabilistic ('more likely') and the boundary permits thermodynamically dominated exceptions, whereas the falsification rule treats one slow-heating comparison as decisively disproving a necessary rapid-processing condition.
